about: Trivia: useful values, by section (the tabs). Each entry has a name, a `short` description (shown in its row) and a `description` (shown when selected), and either a value (with an optional unit and number of decimals), or `between` two places (their distance along the Earth's surface), or `tip` (an example request, written by Enter), or `estimate` + `live` (a spacecraft's distance from Earth: retrieved from JPL Horizons when online, else estimated from `estimate`). To add one, add an object to a section's `entries`. `show`: [unit, unit, …] shows the value in the first unit (written by Enter) and, in brackets, in the second (`["km", "au", "ly"]`); the popup shows it in all of them, its planet distances too; `decimals` applies to the first. `planet`: the popup (Enter) computes its distances from the Sun and the Earth (mean, next minimum and maximum with their dates). `details`: [label, text] lines added to the popup. `satellites` (all, starlink, leo, meo, geo, heo, beyond) + `estimate` {as_of, count}: counted from CelesTrak's active satellites when online, else the estimate. `symbol`: a few characters that recall it, shown beside it; `wikipedia`: a link shown in the popup; `value_label`: the label of the value in the popup (default `Value`).

entries.name: Distance between places
entries.short: Just type the cities from and to
entries.description: Just type the city from and to: London [to] Paris [mi/km/…]. A place can be a capital, a major city, a country or coordinates (41.9,12.5); the distance is along the Earth's surface.

entries.name: Equator
entries.description: The Earth's circumference along the equator (WGS84 ellipsoid).

entries.name: Greenwich meridian
entries.description: The prime meridian from pole to pole through Greenwich; a full meridian circle is 40007.863 km, shorter than the equator because the Earth is flattened.

entries.name: Earth's mean radius
entries.description: The radius of a sphere with the Earth's volume (IUGG).

entries.name: Mount Everest
entries.description: The highest point above sea level (China–Nepal survey, 2020).

entries.name: Voyager 1
entries.description: Space probe launched by NASA in the Voyager program to study the outer Solar System and interstellar space. It flew by Jupiter (1979) and Saturn (1980), crossed into interstellar space on 25 August 2012, and is the farthest human-made object. It still operates and communicates with the Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network.

entries.name: Voyager 2
entries.description: Space probe launched by NASA in the Voyager program, 16 days before Voyager 1. The only probe to have visited Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989), after Jupiter and Saturn; it entered interstellar space on 5 November 2018. It still operates and communicates with the Earth through NASA's Deep Space Network.

entries.name: Moon
entries.description: The Moon orbits the Earth in an ellipse, so its distance from us changes through each month. The mean distance is the semi-major axis of that orbit; light covers it in about 1.28 seconds.
details: between about 356,400 and 370,400 km, every 27.55 days
the Moon moves away by about 3.8 cm a year
about 1.02 km/s (3,680 km/h) around the Earth: 1.08 km/s at perigee, 0.97 at apogee

entries.name: Mercury
entries.description: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, with the most eccentric orbit of the eight: a year of 88 days.
details: 4222.6 h - 175.94 d (two of its years: it turns three times while it goes round the Sun twice)

entries.name: Venus
entries.description: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the one that comes closest to the Earth; its orbit is the most circular of the planets. A year of 225 days.
details: 5832.6 h - 243.025 d (backwards: the Sun rises in the west)

entries.name: Earth
entries.description: The Earth's mean distance from the Sun defines the astronomical unit (au), now fixed at exactly 149,597,870.7 km. Sunlight takes about 8 min 19 s to arrive.
details: 23.9345 h - 0.99727 d (23 h 56 min 4 s, the sidereal day)
24 h - 1 d (on average: the solar day)

entries.name: Mars
entries.description: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. Its orbit is eccentric, so its distance from the Earth at closest approach varies from about 55 to 100 million km. A year of 687 days.

entries.name: Jupiter
entries.description: Jupiter is the largest planet, a gas giant more than twice as massive as all the others together. A year of 11.9 Earth years.
details: 9.925 h - 0.41354 d (9 h 55 min 30 s, the shortest of the planets)

entries.name: Saturn
entries.description: Saturn is the second-largest planet, known for its rings of ice and rock. A year of 29.5 Earth years.

entries.name: Uranus
entries.description: Uranus is an ice giant that rotates on its side, its axis tilted by 98°. A year of 84 Earth years; visited only by Voyager 2 (1986).
details: 17.24 h - 0.71833 d (17 h 14 min 24 s, backwards: it rotates on its side)

entries.name: Neptune
entries.description: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun, an ice giant found in 1846 by mathematical prediction. A year of 165 Earth years; visited only by Voyager 2 (1989).

entries.name: Light-year
entries.short: Distance light travels in a year
entries.description: The distance light travels in vacuum in one Julian year (365.25 days), a unit for distances between stars; the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is 4.24 light-years away.

entries.name: Active satellites
entries.description: Active (working) satellites orbiting the Earth, counted from CelesTrak's catalogue of active payloads; debris and spent rocket bodies are not included.
details: from about 3.07 km/s (11,070 km/h) in the geostationary belt to 7.8 km/s (28,000 km/h) in low orbit

entries.name: Starlink
entries.description: SpaceX's Starlink satellites, in low Earth orbit at about 340–570 km: by far the largest constellation.
details: Low Earth orbit, about 340–570 km, in shells of different inclinations.
about 7.6–7.7 km/s (27,300–27,700 km/h): a lap in about 91–96 minutes

entries.name: Low Earth orbit (LEO)
entries.description: Active satellites whose highest point is below 2,000 km: Earth observation, the ISS, Starlink, OneWeb.
details: Below 2,000 km altitude; a lap takes about 90–127 minutes.

entries.name: Medium Earth orbit (MEO)
entries.description: Active satellites between low Earth orbit and the geostationary belt: navigation (GPS, Galileo, GLONASS, BeiDou) at about 20,000 km, O3b.
details: 2,000 km to just below 35,786 km; GPS orbits at 20,200 km, a lap in 12 hours.

entries.name: Geostationary orbit (GEO)
entries.description: Active satellites in near-circular orbits with a period of one sidereal day, above the equator at 35,786 km: TV, weather, communications.
details: 35,786 km above the equator, a lap in 23 h 56 min: they stay over the same point.
3.07 km/s (11,070 km/h): one turn a day, like the Earth below

entries.name: Highly elliptical orbit (HEO)
entries.description: Active satellites in very eccentric orbits (eccentricity 0.25 or more), such as Molniya and Tundra, which linger over high latitudes.
details: Eccentricity 0.25 or more: low perigee, apogee up to tens of thousands of km.
varies along the orbit: a Molniya about 10 km/s at perigee, 1.5 km/s at apogee

entries.name: Beyond geostationary
entries.description: Active satellites in near-circular orbits beyond the geostationary belt.
details: Apogee above 35,786 km, not geostationary nor highly elliptical.
below 3.07 km/s, slower the farther out

entries.name: π (pi)
entries.description: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
details: Archimedes of Syracuse (c. 250 BC) bounded it between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7; William Jones named it π (1706), and Leonhard Euler made the name standard.
π = C / d, the circumference of any circle over its diameter; also π = 4 (1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − 1/7 + …) (Leibniz).

entries.name: e (Euler's number)
entries.description: The base of the natural logarithm: the limit of (1 + 1/n)^n.
details: Jacob Bernoulli (1683) found it studying compound interest; Leonhard Euler named it e and computed it to 18 decimals (1748).
e = lim (1 + 1/n)^n = 1 + 1/1! + 1/2! + 1/3! + …: the base whose exponential function is its own derivative.

entries.description: The diagonal of a unit square; the first number known to be irrational.
details: The Pythagoreans (traditionally Hippasus of Metapontum, 5th century BC) proved it irrational; a Babylonian tablet (YBC 7289, c. 1700 BC) gives it to six digits.
The positive number whose square is 2: x² = 2; the diagonal of a square of side 1.

entries.name: φ (golden ratio)
entries.description: (1 + √5) / 2: the limit of the ratio of consecutive Fibonacci numbers.
details: Euclid (Elements, c. 300 BC) defined it as the extreme and mean ratio; the letter φ, for the sculptor Phidias, is Mark Barr's (c. 1909).
φ = (1 + √5) / 2, the positive root of x² = x + 1: a line cut so that the whole is to the longer part as the longer is to the shorter.

entries.name: Electronvolt
entries.short: Energy of an electron across 1 volt
entries.description: The energy one electron gains when it crosses a voltage of 1 volt. Physicists use it for the energies of atoms and particles, far too small for joules. Exact since the 2019 redefinition of the SI.
details: a photon carries 1.6 to 3.3 eV (red to violet)
a chemical bond holds a few eV
the LHC gives each proton 6.8 TeV (6.8 million million eV)

entries.name: Speed of light
entries.description: The speed of light and of every electromagnetic wave (radio, X-rays) in a vacuum, and the universe's speed limit: nothing with mass reaches it. Exact since 1983: the metre is the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of a second.

entries.name: Standard gravity
entries.description: How fast an object falling freely near the Earth's surface speeds up, as a standard value: each second its speed grows by about 9.8 m/s (35 km/h). It is the unit g of acceleration, as felt by pilots or on a roller coaster.
details: 9.780 m/s² (the Earth spins and bulges there)

entries.name: Standard atmosphere
entries.description: The average pressure of the air at sea level, a reference unit (1 atm): the weight of the air above each square metre. Weather maps give it in hectopascals; it falls with altitude.

entries.name: Absolute zero
entries.description: The lowest possible temperature, where matter's particles have the least energy they can have: 0 on the Kelvin scale. It can be approached but never reached; laboratories have cooled atoms to a billionth of a degree above it.
details: about 2.7 K, the glow left by the Big Bang

entries.name: Avogadro constant
entries.description: The number of particles (atoms, molecules) in one mole of a substance: chemists count in moles, as bakers in dozens. A mole of water weighs 18 g, about a spoonful. Exact since the 2019 SI.

entries.name: Planck constant
entries.description: The constant of quantum mechanics: light comes in packets (photons), each with the energy E = h·f, f being its frequency. Exact since 2019, when it began to define the kilogram.

entries.name: Men's shoes
entries.description: Nike's men's chart, each row one size in every system and the foot it fits. Other brands cut differently: check the brand's chart. A row writes its request (42 eu men shoes).

entries.name: Women's shoes
entries.description: Nike's women's chart, each row one size in every system and the foot it fits. Other brands cut differently: check the brand's chart. A row writes its request (38 eu women shoes).

entries.name: Kids' shoes
entries.description: Nike's kids' chart: toddler sizes (US C) then youth sizes (US Y), each row one size in every system and the foot it fits. Other brands cut differently: check the brand's chart. A row writes its request (30 eu kids shoes).
